GeneCastR: a short tutorial

This package takes prevalence surveys for a genetic marker – several sites, several years, a count positive out of a number tested – and fits a model of how that marker spreads. From a single fit one can answer questions such as

  • is the marker spreading, and how fast?
  • where is it likely to be in a few years’ time?
  • when did it arrive at each site?

This tutorial works through those three in order, on the example panel supplied with the package. It uses default settings throughout: the surveys go in and nothing else needs choosing.

library(GeneCastR)

The data

Input is one row per survey, with a site, a time, the number positive and the number tested. The example is sixteen Ugandan districts surveyed annually from 2016 to 2022 for the PfKelch13 C469Y artemisinin-resistance marker.

d <- gc_example_data(M = 16)
#> 16 row(s) with n == 0 dropped (no information).
head(d$surveys, 4)
#>    deme time  x  n step          f         lo         hi
#> 1 Agago 2016  0 30   16 0.00000000 0.00000000 0.06151672
#> 2 Agago 2017  2 44   32 0.04545455 0.01315698 0.12016535
#> 3 Agago 2018  1 31   48 0.03225806 0.00570508 0.11934267
#> 4 Agago 2019 10 47   64 0.21276596 0.12864448 0.32229633

gc_example_data() is a convenience wrapper an arbitrary data frame:

d <- GCData$new(surveys, M = 16,
                cols = c(deme = "district", time = "year",
                         x = "n_positive", n = "n_tested"))

where cols says which column is which.

  • time can be a number or a date. A plain 2016 is taken as given. A Date or POSIXct column is converted to a decimal year – 2016-07-01 becomes 2016.497.
  • Rows where nothing was tested are dropped, with a message. Survey extracts routinely carry a row for a site-year that was not sampled.

M sets the time resolution: how many steps the model takes per unit of time. At M = 16 with reports at yearly resolustions, the model moves in roughly \(52/M \approx\) three-week steps. Finer is slower, and the answers stop changing well before the resolution becomes a concern; 16 is a reasonable default for annual data.

d
#> <GCData>
#>   demes    : 16 (Agago, Amolatar, Arua, ...)
#>   surveys  : 96 (42 non-zero)
#>   window   : 2015 to 2022   M = 16, T = 112 steps
#>   never positive: 2 deme(s) -- Jinja, Kanungu

Fitting

Here’s an example of a fit object:

stored <- gc_example_tstar_fit()$panel
fit <- stored$fit
pr <- stored$pr
fit
#> <GCFit>  Poisson flow, t* t_min + negative binomial
#>           (t* = the first non-zero draw)
#>   data    : 16 demes, 96 surveys, M = 16, T = 192
#>   window  : 2010 to 2022, lead-in 96 steps
#>   chains  : 4 x 4000 (2000 warm-up), 8000 draws retained
#>   time    : 415.8 s on 4 cores
#> 
#>           variable  median      q5     q95 rhat ess_bulk
#>                  u  0.1982 -0.0737  0.4407 1.00     1095
#>                  A  0.2193 -0.0711  0.5537 1.00     1095
#>                 nu  0.0275  0.0130  0.0496 1.01     1158
#>              N_eff 14.5036  8.2957 26.8980 1.01      884
#>        tstar_shape  1.6507  1.0650  3.5436 1.01     1231
#>  p_beyond_baseline  0.1057  0.0523  0.1322 1.01     1231

A fit of this size takes several minutes on four cores; this vignette shows a stored result. The call that produced it was

fit <- GCFit$new(d, chains = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, cores = 4,
                 lead_in = 6 * 16,
                 control = gc_control(tstar_min = 2012, tstar_mean = 2017))

chains and iter are the usual Markov chain settings and cores runs the chains in parallel over the number of specified cores. The other three arguments are priors about arrival time:

  • lead_in is how far back before the first survey the model is allowed to look, counted in model steps, so 6 * 16 is six years at M = 16.
  • tstar_min is the earliest year the marker could have arrived anywhere. Nothing before it is entertained.
  • tstar_mean is roughly when arrival is expected, on average across sites.

We can let tstar_min and tstar_mean be deme specific. They take either one value for the whole panel, as above, or one value per site. For per-site values, pass a vector named by site:

fit <- GCFit$new(d, chains = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, cores = 4,
                 lead_in = 6 * 16,
                 control = gc_control(
                   tstar_min  = c(Koboko = 2012, Arua = 2012, Kanungu = 2014),
                   tstar_mean = c(Koboko = 2016, Arua = 2016, Kanungu = 2019)))

The names are checked against the data, and a tstar_min falling after a site’s own first positive survey is refused, since the two would contradict each other. lead_in stays a single number for the panel: it only has to reach back far enough for the earliest tstar_min.

Checking the fit

Two columns of the printout at the start of the Fitting section give an indication of whether the MCMC fit has converged, and whether the estimates that follow should be retained.

rhat compares the four chains. If they explored the same region it sits at 1.00. Anything above about 1.05 means they did not agree and the fit should be run for longer; the printout says so when it happens.

ess_bulk is how many independent draws the correlated ones are worth.

The chains themselves should look like stationary noise with no wandering:

gc_plot_trace(fit)


gc_plot_hist(fit)

The histograms present posterior histograms for each parameter, we should hope for each chain to sit in the same place.

Is the marker spreading?

A is the growth advantage: the proportional change in the marker’s frequency per year that selection buys it. An A of 0.2 is roughly a fifth faster per year than a neutral marker would manage, and an A of zero is no advantage at all.

gc_plot_hist(fit, "A", ncol = 1)


A <- as.numeric(posterior::as_draws_matrix(fit$draws)[, "A"])
round(stats::quantile(A, c(.025, .5, .975)), 3)
#>   2.5%    50%  97.5% 
#> -0.123  0.219  0.628
c(`P(A > 0)` = mean(A > 0), `P(A > 0.25)` = mean(A > 0.25))
#>    P(A > 0) P(A > 0.25) 
#>    0.898625    0.446375

That is the estimate of the advantage, a 95% interval around it, and the probability that there is any advantage at all.

Projections and probability of presence

We can create projections to forecast future frequencies, the object looks like this

pr
#> <GCProjection>
#>   3840 rows: 16 demes x 240 steps (192 smoothed, 48 projected)
#>   window   : 2010.062 to 2025
#>   draws    : 400, 400 paths each
#>   exceedance thresholds: 0.01, 0.05, 0.1
#>   P(t* beyond the record): mean 0.066, max 0.561
#> 
#>   at 2025: mean P(present) 0.825, mean median f 0.106

and is created by running

pr <- fit$project(horizon = 3, n_paths = 400)

horizon = 3 projects three years past the last survey. Inside the survey window the curves are smoothed: every survey at a site, later ones included, informs the estimate at every time. Past the last survey the same model carries that state forward.

gc_plot_frequency(pr)

The probability of presence \(p(k_t>0)\) can by visualised using:

gc_plot_present(pr)

And exceedance probabilities \(p(f_t>\text{threshold})\):

gc_plot_exceed(pr)

All of these can be produced by pr$curves, one row per site and time step, for the numbers rather than the pictures:

head(pr$curves[, c("deme", "time", "f_mean", "p_present", "p_exceed_5")], 4)
#>    deme     time f_mean    p_present p_exceed_5
#> 1 Agago 2010.062      0 1.970646e-17          0
#> 2 Agago 2010.125      0 1.887379e-17          0
#> 3 Agago 2010.188      0 1.720846e-17          0
#> 4 Agago 2010.250      0 1.942890e-17          0

Note that presence need not rise steadily. It dips between surveys and recovers at each positive one, again because the marker can die out locally and return.

When did it arrive?

There are two distinct answers here, and conflating them is the commonest mistake made with this model.

t* is when the marker first reached the site, ever – including arrivals that died out without ever being seen.

T_est is when the lineage that was actually detected got started. Walk back from the first positive survey until the site is empty; that is where the detected marker began.

The two events differ whenever a marker arrived, died out, and arrived again.

gc_plot_times(pr, "cdf")

Each curve climbs to one and stops at the dashed line, the first positive survey. That line is a hard limit: whatever was detected must have started before it was detected.

The gap between the curves is turnover. Where they nearly coincide, the marker was found soon after it arrived. Where the green curve climbs years before the purple one, the marker was probably present long before the lineage that was caught, and whatever came first died out. Sites never found positive have no purple curve at all – there is no detected lineage to date.

gc_plot_times(pr, "pmf")

The same information as densities.

Further reading

fit$summary()        # the table printed above
fit$draws            # every posterior draw, as a posterior package object
pr$curves            # one row per site and time step
pr$demes             # one row per site
